Simple Machines.correct_answer: Some input energy is always lost to friction and other resistive forces, rather than being entirely converted into useful output work

Simple Machines.text: A single fixed pulley provides which of the following primary benefits?
options: A significant mechanical advantage greater than 1
A change in the direction of the applied force, though generally with a mechanical advantage close to 1
No practical benefit whatsoever
An automatic increase in the load’s weight
Simple Machines.correct_answer: A change in the direction of the applied force, though generally with a mechanical advantage close to 1

Simple Machines.text: A block-and-tackle (multiple pulley) system provides mechanical advantage mainly by
options: using several pulleys and rope segments to share the load’s weight across multiple supporting strands
using a single rope with no additional pulleys
increasing the load’s weight directly
having no relationship between the number of pulleys and mechanical advantage
Simple Machines.correct_answer: using several pulleys and rope segments to share the load’s weight across multiple supporting strands

Simple Machines.text: Which of the following correctly identifies why gears are considered examples of simple machines?
options: They transmit and can modify rotational force and speed between connected shafts, similar in principle to a wheel and axle system
Gears have no relationship to simple machine principles
Gears can only reduce mechanical advantage, never increase it
Gears operate purely on optical principles
Simple Machines.correct_answer: They transmit and can modify rotational force and speed between connected shafts, similar in principle to a wheel and axle system

Simple Machines.text: Which of the following correctly explains why a longer inclined plane (ramp), for a given height, generally requires a smaller effort force to move a load up it, compared to a shorter, steeper ramp?
options: A longer ramp has a smaller angle of inclination, spreading the same work over a greater distance and therefore requiring a smaller effort force
Ramp length has no effect on the required effort force
A longer ramp always requires more effort, not less
Effort force is completely unrelated to a ramp’s length or angle
Simple Machines.correct_answer: A longer ramp has a smaller angle of inclination, spreading the same work over a greater distance and therefore requiring a smaller effort force

Simple Machines.text: Which of the following correctly explains why simple machines, despite reducing the effort force needed, do not reduce the total work that must be done to raise a given load through a given height (ignoring friction)?
options: By the principle of conservation of energy, any reduction in effort force is compensated by an increased distance over which the effort must act, keeping total work roughly constant (for an ideal, frictionless machine)
Simple machines always reduce the total work required, violating energy conservation
Work done is entirely independent of both force and distance moved
There is no relationship between effort force, distance, and total work done
Simple Machines.correct_answer: By the principle of conservation of energy, any reduction in effort force is compensated by an increased distance over which the effort must act, keeping total work roughly constant (for an ideal, frictionless machine)

Simple Machines.text: Which of the following correctly explains a practical everyday application of the lever principle?
options: Using a crowbar to lift a heavy object, applying a smaller effort force over a larger distance from the fulcrum than the load’s distance
Levers have no everyday practical applications
Levers can only be used in highly specialized industrial equipment
The lever principle is unrelated to how a crowbar functions
Simple Machines.correct_answer: Using a crowbar to lift a heavy object, applying a smaller effort force over a larger distance from the fulcrum than the load’s distance

Simple Machines.text: Which of the following correctly explains why hydraulic systems (such as hydraulic jacks) are considered simple machines that provide significant mechanical advantage?
options: A small force applied over a large area on one side of the system can produce a much larger force over a smaller area on the other side, based on Pascal’s principle
Hydraulic systems have no relationship to simple machine principles
Hydraulic jacks always require more effort than the load being lifted, with no mechanical advantage
Pascal’s principle is unrelated to how hydraulic systems provide mechanical advantage
Simple Machines.correct_answer: A small force applied over a large area on one side of the system can produce a much larger force over a smaller area on the other side, based on Pascal’s principle

Simple Machines.text: Which of the following correctly explains why lubricating the moving parts of a machine generally improves its efficiency?
options: Lubrication reduces frictional losses, allowing a greater proportion of input energy to be converted into useful output work
Lubrication has no effect on machine efficiency
Lubrication always decreases machine efficiency
Friction has no relationship to machine efficiency
Simple Machines.correct_answer: Lubrication reduces frictional losses, allowing a greater proportion of input energy to be converted into useful output work

Simple Machines.text: Which of the following correctly explains why understanding mechanical advantage and velocity ratio is important when selecting an appropriate machine for a specific practical task?
options: It allows an appropriate trade-off between the effort force required and the distance/speed of application, matching the machine to the specific requirements of the task
Mechanical advantage and velocity ratio have no relevance to selecting a machine for a task
All simple machines provide identical mechanical advantage regardless of design
Velocity ratio has no bearing on how a machine should be selected for a task
Simple Machines.correct_answer: It allows an appropriate trade-off between the effort force required and the distance/speed of application, matching the machine to the specific requirements of the task

Simple Machines.text: Which of the following correctly summarizes the overall importance of simple machines in engineering and everyday life?
options: They enable tasks requiring large forces or precise motion control to be accomplished more easily, underpinning countless mechanical devices and systems
Simple machines have no significant role in engineering or everyday life
Simple machine principles apply only to purely theoretical physics problems
Modern engineering has entirely superseded the relevance of simple machine principles
Simple Machines.correct_answer: They enable tasks requiring large forces or precise motion control to be accomplished more easily, underpinning countless mechanical devices and systems

Elasticity.text: Elasticity refers to a material’s ability to
options: permanently deform under any applied force
return to its original shape and size after a deforming force is removed
break immediately when any force is applied
never deform under any circumstances
Elasticity.correct_answer: return to its original shape and size after a deforming force is removed

Elasticity.text: The elastic limit of a material is the point beyond which
options: the material returns to its original shape upon removal of the force
the material no longer returns completely to its original shape when the deforming force is removed; permanent deformation begins
the material cannot be deformed at all
Hooke’s law applies indefinitely, with no limit
Elasticity.correct_answer: the material no longer returns completely to its original shape when the deforming force is removed; permanent deformation begins

Elasticity.text: Hooke’s law states that, within the elastic limit, the extension of a material is
options: inversely proportional to the applied force
directly proportional to the applied force
completely independent of the applied force
always equal to zero
Elasticity.correct_answer: directly proportional to the applied force

Elasticity.text: The yield point of a material refers to the point at which
options: the material begins to extend significantly with little or no further increase in applied force
the material first begins to be deformed at all
the material becomes completely rigid
elastic behaviour is guaranteed to continue indefinitely
Elasticity.correct_answer: the material begins to extend significantly with little or no further increase in applied force

Elasticity.text: The breaking point of a material refers to the point at which
options: the material returns to its original shape
the material actually fractures or breaks under the applied force
the material becomes more elastic than before
Hooke’s law begins to apply
Elasticity.correct_answer: the material actually fractures or breaks under the applied force

Elasticity.text: Young’s modulus of a material is defined as the ratio of
options: extension to original length
stress to strain, within the elastic limit
force to extension only, without reference to dimensions
mass to volume
Elasticity.correct_answer: stress to strain, within the elastic limit

Elasticity.text: A spring balance is a practical device used to measure
options: mass directly, without any reference to force
force (or weight), based on the extension of a calibrated spring, applying Hooke’s law
volume of liquids
electrical resistance
Elasticity.correct_answer: force (or weight), based on the extension of a calibrated spring, applying Hooke’s law

Elasticity.text: The work done in stretching a spring or elastic string, within its elastic limit, can be calculated as the area under a
options: force-time graph
force-extension graph
velocity-time graph
temperature- time graph
Elasticity.correct_answer: force-extension graph

Elasticity.text: For a spring obeying Hooke’s law, the work done in stretching it by an extension x, with spring constant k, is given by
options: kx
½kx²
kx²
k/x
Elasticity.correct_answer: ½kx²

Elasticity.text: Stress, in the context of elasticity, is defined as
options: force per unit cross-sectional area
extension per unit original length
force multiplied by extension
mass per unit volume
Elasticity.correct_answer: force per unit cross-sectional area

Elasticity.text: Strain, in the context of elasticity, is defined as
options: force per unit area
extension (or change in length) per unit original length
force multiplied by length
mass per unit length
Elasticity.correct_answer: extension (or change in length) per unit original length

Elasticity.text: A material that obeys Hooke’s law shows a force-extension graph that is
options: a curve throughout
a straight line through the origin, up to the elastic limit
always horizontal
always vertical
Elasticity.correct_answer: a straight line through the origin, up to the elastic limit

Elasticity.text: Which of the following materials would typically be described as “ductile,” able to be stretched significantly before breaking?
options: Glass
Copper wire
Ceramic
Cast iron, generally
Elasticity.correct_answer: Copper wire

Elasticity.text: Which of the following materials would typically be described as “brittle,” breaking with little prior deformation?
options: Rubber
Copper
Glass
Steel wire, generally
Elasticity.correct_answer: Glass

Elasticity.text: Which of the following correctly explains why extending a spring beyond its elastic limit results in permanent deformation?
options: Beyond the elastic limit, the internal structure of the material is permanently altered, so it no longer returns completely to its original shape when the force is removed
The elastic limit has no relationship to permanent deformation
Materials always return fully to their original shape regardless of how far they are stretched
Permanent deformation occurs only below the elastic limit
Elasticity.correct_answer: Beyond the elastic limit, the internal structure of the material is permanently altered, so it no longer returns completely to its original shape when the force is removed

Elasticity.text: Which of the following correctly explains why Young’s modulus is considered a property of the material itself, rather than of a specific object made from that material?
options: Young’s modulus, being derived from stress and strain (which account for cross-sectional area and original length), gives a value independent of the specific dimensions of a particular sample
Young’s modulus always changes significantly with the specific size or shape of an object
Young’s modulus depends only on the object’s mass, not on the material’s inherent properties
There is no meaningful distinction between a material’s Young’s modulus and an object’s specific stiffness
Elasticity.correct_answer: Young’s modulus, being derived from stress and strain (which account for cross-sectional area and original length), gives a value independent of the specific dimensions of a particular sample

Elasticity.text: Which of the following correctly explains why a spring balance can be reliably used to measure force, provided it is used within its elastic limit?
options: Within the elastic limit, extension is directly proportional to applied force (Hooke’s law), allowing a calibrated scale to accurately relate extension to force
Spring balances work equally reliably regardless of whether they are used within or beyond the elastic limit
There is no relationship between a spring’s extension and the applied force
Spring balances measure mass directly, with no relevance to force or extension
Elasticity.correct_answer: Within the elastic limit, extension is directly proportional to applied force (Hooke’s law), allowing a calibrated scale to accurately relate extension to force

Elasticity.text: Which of the following correctly explains why steel cables used in suspension bridges must be selected with careful consideration of their elastic properties and breaking strength?
options: The cables must safely support significant loads while remaining within their elastic limit under normal conditions, and must have a breaking strength well above the maximum expected load, for safety
Elastic properties and breaking strength are irrelevant to suspension bridge cable selection
Suspension bridge cables are always selected without regard to potential loads
Breaking strength has no relevance to structural safety considerations
Elasticity.correct_answer: The cables must safely support significant loads while remaining within their elastic limit under normal conditions, and must have a breaking strength well above the maximum expected load, for safety

Elasticity.text: Which of the following correctly explains why a rubber band, unlike a metal spring, often shows significant deviation from Hooke’s law (a non-linear force-extension relationship) even at relatively small extensions?
options: Rubber’s molecular structure (long, coiled polymer chains) behaves differently under stress than the crystalline lattice structure of most metals, leading to more complex, non-linear elastic behaviour
Rubber always follows Hooke’s law perfectly, identically to metal springs
There is no structural difference between rubber and metal relevant to their elastic behaviour
Metals never follow Hooke’s law, unlike rubber
Elasticity.correct_answer: Rubber’s molecular structure (long, coiled polymer chains) behaves differently under stress than the crystalline lattice structure of most metals, leading to more complex, non-linear elastic behaviour

Elasticity.text: Which of the following correctly explains the practical importance of understanding elastic energy storage (as in a stretched spring or elastic string) in devices such as archery bows or catapults?
options: The elastic potential energy stored during stretching is converted into kinetic energy upon release, propelling a projectile
Elastic energy storage has no practical relevance to devices such as bows or catapults
Bows and catapults function through purely magnetic principles, unrelated to elasticity
Stretching a bowstring does not involve any elastic potential energy
Elasticity.correct_answer: The elastic potential energy stored during stretching is converted into kinetic energy upon release, propelling a projectile

Elasticity.text: Which of the following correctly explains why engineers need to know a material’s elastic limit and Young’s modulus when designing structural components, such as building beams?
options: This information allows engineers to predict how much a component will deform under expected loads, and ensures the component remains within its elastic (safe, recoverable) range during normal use
Elastic limit and Young’s modulus have no relevance to structural engineering design
Structural components are always designed without any reference to material elastic properties
Beams deform identically regardless of the specific material’s elastic properties
Elasticity.correct_answer: This information allows engineers to predict how much a component will deform under expected loads, and ensures the component remains within its elastic (safe, recoverable) range during normal use

Elasticity.text: Which of the following correctly explains why two springs of identical material but different coil geometry (such as different wire thickness or coil diameter) can have different spring constants, despite being made of the same material?
options: The spring constant depends not only on the material’s inherent elastic properties but also on the specific geometry of the spring, such as wire thickness, coil diameter, and number of coils
Spring constant depends only on the material, never on the specific geometry of the spring
All springs made of the same material always have identical spring constants
Geometry has no bearing on a spring’s mechanical behaviour
Elasticity.correct_answer: The spring constant depends not only on the material’s inherent elastic properties but also on the specific geometry of the spring, such as wire thickness, coil diameter, and number of coils

Elasticity.text: Which of the following correctly explains why repeatedly stretching a material beyond its elastic limit, even without immediately breaking it, can eventually weaken the material (a phenomenon related to fatigue)?
options: Repeated plastic (permanent) deformation can introduce microscopic structural damage that accumulates over time, eventually reducing the material’s strength and increasing the likelihood of failure
Repeated stretching beyond the elastic limit has no cumulative effect on material strength
Materials always become stronger when repeatedly stretched beyond their elastic limit
Fatigue has no relationship to a material’s elastic limit
Elasticity.correct_answer: Repeated plastic (permanent) deformation can introduce microscopic structural damage that accumulates over time, eventually reducing the material’s strength and increasing the likelihood of failure

Elasticity.text: Which of the following correctly summarizes the overall importance of studying elasticity, Hooke’s law, and Young’s modulus in physics and engineering?
options: These concepts underpin the design and safety analysis of countless structures and devices, from simple springs to major engineering structures, ensuring materials perform reliably under expected loads
Elasticity concepts have no meaningful application in engineering or structural design
Hooke’s law and Young’s modulus are relevant only to purely theoretical physics with no practical use
Structural safety analysis requires no consideration of a material’s elastic properties
Elasticity.correct_answer: These concepts underpin the design and safety analysis of countless structures and devices, from simple springs to major engineering structures, ensuring materials perform reliably under expected loads

Pressure.text: Atmospheric pressure is defined as the
options: pressure exerted by a liquid at a given depth
pressure exerted by the weight of the air (atmosphere) above a given point
pressure inside a sealed container only
pressure exerted only at sea level, never varying
Pressure.correct_answer: pressure exerted by the weight of the air (atmosphere) above a given point

Pressure.text: The SI unit of pressure is the
options: newton
pascal
joule
watt
Pressure.correct_answer: pascal

Pressure.text: A simple mercury barometer is used to measure
options: temperature
atmospheric pressure
humidity directly
the speed of sound
Pressure.correct_answer: atmospheric pressure

Pressure.text: An aneroid barometer measures atmospheric pressure using
options: a column of mercury
the mechanical response (expansion/contraction) of a partially evacuated flexible metal chamber
a column of water
an electrical resistance thermometer
Pressure.correct_answer: the mechanical response (expansion/contraction) of a partially evacuated flexible metal chamber

Pressure.text: A manometer is used to measure
options: temperature
the pressure difference between a gas and the atmosphere, typically using a liquid column
humidity
time intervals
Pressure.correct_answer: the pressure difference between a gas and the atmosphere, typically using a liquid column

Pressure.text: As altitude above sea level increases, atmospheric pressure generally
options: increases
decreases, since there is progressively less air above a given point
remains constant everywhere
becomes negative
Pressure.correct_answer: decreases, since there is progressively less air above a given point

Pressure.text: A barometer can be used as an altimeter because
options: atmospheric pressure has no relationship to altitude
atmospheric pressure decreases in a predictable way with increasing altitude, allowing altitude to be estimated from pressure readings
altitude has no effect on barometric readings
barometers can only measure temperature, not pressure
Pressure.correct_answer: atmospheric pressure decreases in a predictable way with increasing altitude, allowing altitude to be estimated from pressure readings

Pressure.text: The pressure at a depth h in a liquid of density ρ is given by the expression
options: P = ρg/h
P = ρgh
P = ρ/gh
P = gh/ρ
Pressure.correct_answer: P = ρgh

Pressure.text: According to the pressure-depth-density relationship, pressure in a liquid increases with
options: decreasing depth
increasing depth (and increasing density), for a given location
decreasing density only
no dependence on depth or density
Pressure.correct_answer: increasing depth (and increasing density), for a given location

Pressure.text: Pascal’s principle states that pressure applied to an enclosed, incompressible fluid is
options: absorbed entirely at the point of application, with no transmission elsewhere
transmitted equally in all directions throughout the fluid
only transmitted downward
reduced significantly as it moves through the fluid
Pressure.correct_answer: transmitted equally in all directions throughout the fluid

Pressure.text: A hydraulic press or hydraulic jack operates based on
options: Boyle’s law
Pascal’s principle of pressure transmission in an enclosed fluid
Archimedes’ principle
Newton’s third law only, with no reference to fluid pressure
Pressure.correct_answer: Pascal’s principle of pressure transmission in an enclosed fluid

Pressure.text: Which of the following correctly explains why a hydraulic jack can lift a heavy vehicle using a relatively small applied force?
options: A small force applied over a small piston area creates a pressure that, transmitted equally throughout the fluid, produces a much larger force over a larger piston area
Hydraulic jacks work through a purely mechanical lever system, unrelated to fluid pressure
The applied force is always exactly equal to the force lifting the load, providing no mechanical advantage
Fluid pressure has no role in the operation of a hydraulic jack
Pressure.correct_answer: A small force applied over a small piston area creates a pressure that, transmitted equally throughout the fluid, produces a much larger force over a larger piston area

Pressure.text: Which of the following correctly explains why deep-sea divers experience significantly higher pressure than swimmers near the water’s surface?
options: Pressure in a liquid increases with depth, due to the increasing weight of the liquid column above a given point
Pressure in a liquid is completely independent of depth
Pressure decreases with increasing depth in a liquid
Only the density of water, not depth, determines pressure at any point
Pressure.correct_answer: Pressure in a liquid increases with depth, due to the increasing weight of the liquid column above a given point

Pressure.text: Which of the following correctly explains the working principle of a simple mercury barometer for measuring atmospheric pressure?
options: Atmospheric pressure supports a column of mercury in an inverted, sealed tube; the height of this mercury column is directly related to the atmospheric pressure
A mercury barometer measures pressure by directly weighing the mercury on a scale
The height of mercury in a barometer is completely unrelated to atmospheric pressure
Mercury barometers can only be used to measure liquid pressure, not atmospheric pressure
Pressure.correct_answer: Atmospheric pressure supports a column of mercury in an inverted, sealed tube; the height of this mercury column is directly related to the atmospheric pressure

Pressure.text: Which of the following correctly explains why aircraft cabins are pressurized during high-altitude flight?
options: Atmospheric pressure at high altitude is too low to support normal human respiration and comfort, so cabin pressurization maintains conditions closer to those at lower, more comfortable altitudes
Cabin pressurization has no relationship to atmospheric pressure at altitude
Atmospheric pressure increases significantly with altitude, requiring pressure reduction inside the cabin
Pressurization is used only for temperature control, with no relevance to pressure itself
Pressure.correct_answer: Atmospheric pressure at high altitude is too low to support normal human respiration and comfort, so cabin pressurization maintains conditions closer to those at lower, more comfortable altitudes

Pressure.text: Which of the following correctly explains why a drinking straw allows liquid to be drawn upward into the mouth?
options: Sucking reduces the pressure inside the straw below atmospheric pressure, allowing the greater atmospheric pressure acting on the liquid’s surface to push the liquid up into the straw
Liquid rises in a straw due to gravity alone, with no relevance to pressure differences
Atmospheric pressure has no role in how a drinking straw functions
Straws work by creating a vacuum that pulls liquid upward with no involvement of atmospheric pressure
Pressure.correct_answer: Sucking reduces the pressure inside the straw below atmospheric pressure, allowing the greater atmospheric pressure acting on the liquid’s surface to push the liquid up into the straw

Pressure.text: Which of the following correctly explains why a manometer connected to a gas supply can indicate whether the gas pressure is above or below atmospheric pressure?
options: The direction and magnitude of the liquid level difference in the manometer’s two arms directly indicate whether gas pressure exceeds or is less than atmospheric pressure, and by how much
A manometer can only measure pressures exactly equal to atmospheric pressure
Manometers provide no information about the relationship between gas pressure and atmospheric pressure
The liquid level in a manometer is unrelated to the pressure of the connected gas
Pressure.correct_answer: The direction and magnitude of the liquid level difference in the manometer’s two arms directly indicate whether gas pressure exceeds or is less than atmospheric pressure, and by how much

Pressure.text: Which of the following correctly explains why the choice of liquid used in a barometer (such as mercury rather than water) significantly affects the practical height of the barometer column?
options: A denser liquid, such as mercury, requires a much shorter column height to balance a given atmospheric pressure compared to a less dense liquid, such as water
The density of the barometric liquid has no bearing on the required column height
Water would require a shorter column than mercury to balance the same atmospheric pressure
All liquids require an identical column height, regardless of density, to balance atmospheric pressure
Pressure.correct_answer: A denser liquid, such as mercury, requires a much shorter column height to balance a given atmospheric pressure compared to a less dense liquid, such as water

Pressure.text: Which of the following correctly explains why submarines must be structurally designed to withstand significant external pressure at depth?
options: Water pressure increases substantially with depth, exerting considerable inward force on a submarine’s hull, requiring robust structural design to prevent collapse
Water pressure decreases with depth, so submarines require no special structural reinforcement
Pressure at depth has no relevance to submarine hull design
Submarine hulls experience no external pressure regardless of depth
Pressure.correct_answer: Water pressure increases substantially with depth, exerting considerable inward force on a submarine’s hull, requiring robust structural design to prevent collapse

Pressure.text: Which of the following correctly explains why the reading on an aneroid barometer changes as weather conditions change, even without a change in altitude?
options: Atmospheric pressure fluctuates with weather systems (such as high and low pressure systems), and an aneroid barometer’s flexible chamber responds to these pressure changes
Aneroid barometers are unaffected by any changes in atmospheric pressure
Weather conditions have no relationship to atmospheric pressure
Aneroid barometers can only detect changes in temperature, not pressure
Pressure.correct_answer: Atmospheric pressure fluctuates with weather systems (such as high and low pressure systems), and an aneroid barometer’s flexible chamber responds to these pressure changes

Pressure.text: Which of the following correctly explains why the pressure at the bottom of two containers with the same liquid and depth, but very different base areas, would be identical, despite potentially very different total force on the base?
options: Liquid pressure depends only on depth and density (and gravitational field strength), not on the total area of the container base, even though total force (pressure × area) may differ
Liquid pressure always depends primarily on the base area of the container, not on depth
Containers with different base areas always have different pressures at the same depth, regardless of liquid or depth
Pressure and force are identical concepts with no meaningful distinction
Pressure.correct_answer: Liquid pressure depends only on depth and density (and gravitational field strength), not on the total area of the container base, even though total force (pressure × area) may differ

Pressure.text: Which of the following correctly explains why hydraulic brake systems in vehicles rely on the incompressibility of the brake fluid?
options: Because the fluid is essentially incompressible, pressure applied at the brake pedal is transmitted almost instantaneously and effectively throughout the system to the brake pads
Hydraulic brake fluid is highly compressible, which is essential for effective braking
The incompressibility of brake fluid has no relevance to how hydraulic brakes function
Hydraulic brakes function through purely mechanical means, with no involvement of fluid pressure transmission
Pressure.correct_answer: Because the fluid is essentially incompressible, pressure applied at the brake pedal is transmitted almost instantaneously and effectively throughout the system to the brake pads

Pressure.text: Which of the following correctly explains why water towers are typically built at significant height above the areas they supply?
options: The height difference creates sufficient water pressure, due to the depth-pressure relationship, to deliver an adequate water supply through pipes to consumers, without requiring continuous pumping
Water tower height has no relationship to the pressure delivered to consumers
Water towers are built at height purely for aesthetic reasons, unrelated to pressure considerations
Pressure delivered to consumers is completely independent of the water tower’s height
Pressure.correct_answer: The height difference creates sufficient water pressure, due to the depth-pressure relationship, to deliver an adequate water supply through pipes to consumers, without requiring continuous pumping

Pressure.text: Which of the following correctly summarizes the overall importance of understanding pressure concepts (atmospheric pressure, liquid pressure, and Pascal’s principle) in engineering and everyday technology?
options: These concepts underpin technologies ranging from hydraulic systems and aircraft design to water supply systems and weather forecasting instruments
Pressure concepts have no practical relevance to engineering or everyday technology
Only theoretical physics benefits from understanding pressure, with no real-world engineering applications
Atmospheric and liquid pressure concepts are entirely unrelated to practical technology
Pressure.correct_answer: These concepts underpin technologies ranging from hydraulic systems and aircraft design to water supply systems and weather forecasting instruments

Liquids at Rest.text: Density is defined as
options: mass per unit volume of a substance
volume per unit mass of a substance
weight per unit area
mass multiplied by volume
Liquids at Rest.correct_answer: mass per unit volume of a substance

Liquids at Rest.text: Relative density (specific gravity) of a substance is defined as the ratio of
options: its density to the density of water (at a specified reference temperature)
its mass to its volume directly, without any reference substance
its weight to its mass
its volume to the volume of an equal mass of water
Liquids at Rest.correct_answer: its density to the density of water (at a specified reference temperature)

Liquids at Rest.text: Upthrust on a body immersed in a liquid refers to the
options: downward force exerted by the liquid on the body
upward force exerted by the liquid on the body, opposing its weight
force exerted only on floating bodies, never on submerged ones
force that always equals the body’s actual weight, regardless of the liquid
Liquids at Rest.correct_answer: upward force exerted by the liquid on the body, opposing its weight

Liquids at Rest.text: Archimedes’ principle states that the upthrust on a body wholly or partially immersed in a fluid equals the
options: weight of the body itself
weight of the fluid displaced by the body
volume of the body
density of the fluid alone, without reference to volume displaced
Liquids at Rest.correct_answer: weight of the fluid displaced by the body

Liquids at Rest.text: The law of floatation states that a floating body displaces a weight of fluid equal to
options: its own volume
its own weight
the density of the fluid
twice its own weight
Liquids at Rest.correct_answer: its own weight

Liquids at Rest.text: A body floats in a liquid when its average density is
options: greater than the density of the liquid
less than or equal to the density of the liquid
always exactly equal to the density of air
completely unrelated to the liquid’s density
Liquids at Rest.correct_answer: less than or equal to the density of the liquid

Liquids at Rest.text: A body sinks in a liquid when its average density is
options: less than the density of the liquid
greater than the density of the liquid
exactly equal to the density of the liquid
unrelated to the liquid’s density
Liquids at Rest.correct_answer: greater than the density of the liquid

Liquids at Rest.text: A hydrometer is an instrument used to measure the
options: temperature of a liquid
relative density (specific gravity) of a liquid
viscosity of a liquid only
volume of a liquid directly
Liquids at Rest.correct_answer: relative density (specific gravity) of a liquid

Liquids at Rest.text: A hydrometer floats higher in a liquid of
options: lower density
higher density
it floats at the same level regardless of liquid density
it always sinks completely, regardless of density
Liquids at Rest.correct_answer: higher density

Liquids at Rest.text: Ships, despite being made largely of dense steel, are able to float because
options: steel itself has a density lower than water
the overall (average) density of the ship’s hull shape, including the enclosed air space, is less than the density of water
ships always sink, contrary to common observation
floatation has no relationship to average density
Liquids at Rest.correct_answer: the overall (average) density of the ship’s hull shape, including the enclosed air space, is less than the density of water

Liquids at Rest.text: The density of a regularly shaped solid can be determined by
options: measuring its mass and calculating its volume from its dimensions
measuring only its mass, with no reference to volume
measuring only its dimensions, with no reference to mass
it cannot be determined experimentally
Liquids at Rest.correct_answer: measuring its mass and calculating its volume from its dimensions

Liquids at Rest.text: The density of an irregularly shaped solid can be determined by
options: measuring its mass, and determining its volume by liquid displacement
measuring only its length
it cannot be determined at all
using a thermometer exclusively
Liquids at Rest.correct_answer: measuring its mass, and determining its volume by liquid displacement

Liquids at Rest.text: According to Archimedes’ principle, if a body of volume V is completely submerged in a liquid of density ρ, the upthrust it experiences is
options: V/ρ
Vρg
V + ρ
ρg/V
Liquids at Rest.correct_answer: Vρg

Liquids at Rest.text: Which of the following correctly explains why a solid piece of iron sinks in water, while a hollow iron ship floats?
options: The hollow ship’s overall shape displaces a much larger volume of water for the same mass of material, reducing its average density below that of water, unlike the solid iron piece
Solid iron and a hollow iron ship have identical average densities
Iron always floats regardless of its shape
The shape of an object has no bearing on whether it floats or sinks
Liquids at Rest.correct_answer: The hollow ship’s overall shape displaces a much larger volume of water for the same mass of material, reducing its average density below that of water, unlike the solid iron piece

Liquids at Rest.text: Which of the following correctly explains why a hydrometer used for measuring the density of battery acid (or other specific liquids) is calibrated with a specific scale?
options: The hydrometer’s floating depth corresponds directly to the density of the surrounding liquid, allowing a calibrated scale to give a direct density (or concentration) reading
Hydrometers give no useful information about liquid density
A hydrometer’s floating depth is unrelated to the liquid’s density
Hydrometers can only be used with pure water, never other liquids
Liquids at Rest.correct_answer: The hydrometer’s floating depth corresponds directly to the density of the surrounding liquid, allowing a calibrated scale to give a direct density (or concentration) reading

Liquids at Rest.text: Which of the following correctly explains why a person floats more easily in the Dead Sea (which has very high salinity) compared to typical seawater?
options: The Dead Sea’s much higher density, due to its high salt concentration, provides greater upthrust for a given submerged body volume, making floating easier
The Dead Sea has a lower density than ordinary seawater, making floating harder
Salinity has no effect on a liquid’s density or the resulting upthrust
People float equally easily in all bodies of water, regardless of salinity
Liquids at Rest.correct_answer: The Dead Sea’s much higher density, due to its high salt concentration, provides greater upthrust for a given submerged body volume, making floating easier

Liquids at Rest.text: Which of the following correctly explains the practical use of Archimedes’ principle in submarine buoyancy control?
options: Submarines adjust their average density, by controlling the amount of water or air in their ballast tanks, to control whether they float, sink, or remain neutrally buoyant, based on the resulting upthrust relative to weight
Submarines have no ability to control their buoyancy
Archimedes’ principle is unrelated to submarine design or operation
Submarines always sink regardless of their ballast tank configuration
Liquids at Rest.correct_answer: Submarines adjust their average density, by controlling the amount of water or air in their ballast tanks, to control whether they float, sink, or remain neutrally buoyant, based on the resulting upthrust relative to weight

Liquids at Rest.text: Which of the following correctly explains why measuring relative density, rather than absolute density alone, is often practically convenient?
options: Relative density is a dimensionless ratio compared to a common reference (usually water), making comparisons between substances straightforward without needing to track units
Relative density has no practical advantage over absolute density measurements
Relative density cannot be meaningfully compared between different substances
Absolute density measurements are always simpler and more useful than relative density
Liquids at Rest.correct_answer: Relative density is a dimensionless ratio compared to a common reference (usually water), making comparisons between substances straightforward without needing to track units

Liquids at Rest.text: Which of the following correctly explains why an object that is neutrally buoyant in water (neither floating to the surface nor sinking to the bottom) has an average density equal to that of the surrounding water?
options: At neutral buoyancy, the upward Archimedes’ upthrust exactly balances the object’s weight, which occurs specifically when the object’s average density matches the liquid’s density
Neutral buoyancy occurs only when an object’s density is much greater than the liquid’s density
Neutral buoyancy has no relationship to the comparison between object and liquid density
An object can only achieve neutral buoyancy if it has zero mass
Liquids at Rest.correct_answer: At neutral buoyancy, the upward Archimedes’ upthrust exactly balances the object’s weight, which occurs specifically when the object’s average density matches the liquid’s density

Liquids at Rest.text: Which of the following correctly explains why a fish can control its depth in water using an internal swim bladder?
options: By adjusting the amount of gas in its swim bladder, a fish can change its overall body volume and therefore its average density, allowing it to rise, sink, or remain at a constant depth
A fish’s swim bladder has no effect on its buoyancy or depth control
Fish control their depth entirely through muscular swimming effort, with no role for buoyancy adjustment
Swim bladders only function to help fish breathe, with no relevance to buoyancy
Liquids at Rest.correct_answer: By adjusting the amount of gas in its swim bladder, a fish can change its overall body volume and therefore its average density, allowing it to rise, sink, or remain at a constant depth

Liquids at Rest.text: Which of the following correctly explains why hot air balloons rise into the air?
options: Heating the air inside the balloon reduces its density below that of the surrounding cooler air, so the resulting upthrust exceeds the combined weight of the balloon, basket, and heated air
Hot air balloons rise due to a chemical reaction, unrelated to density differences
Heated air always has a higher density than surrounding cooler air
The rising of hot air balloons has no relationship to Archimedes’ principle
Liquids at Rest.correct_answer: Heating the air inside the balloon reduces its density below that of the surrounding cooler air, so the resulting upthrust exceeds the combined weight of the balloon, basket, and heated air

Liquids at Rest.text: Which of the following correctly explains why icebergs float with most of their volume submerged beneath the water’s surface?
options: Ice has a density only slightly less than that of liquid water, so only a relatively small proportion of the iceberg’s volume needs to be above the surface to provide sufficient upthrust to support its weight
Ice has a much lower density than water, so most of an iceberg’s volume is typically above the surface
Icebergs float with their entire volume above the water’s surface
The proportion of an iceberg above versus below the surface has no relationship to relative density
Liquids at Rest.correct_answer: Ice has a density only slightly less than that of liquid water, so only a relatively small proportion of the iceberg’s volume needs to be above the surface to provide sufficient upthrust to support its weight

Liquids at Rest.text: Which of the following correctly explains why accurately determining the density of an irregularly shaped object, such as a small rock, typically requires the liquid displacement method rather than simple geometric calculation?
options: Irregular shapes do not have simple geometric formulas for volume, so displacement of a known volume of liquid provides a practical way to determine the object’s volume, and hence its density
Irregularly shaped objects always have a simple, calculable geometric volume
The liquid displacement method cannot be used for irregularly shaped objects
Density of an irregular object cannot be determined by any practical experimental method
Liquids at Rest.correct_answer: Irregular shapes do not have simple geometric formulas for volume, so displacement of a known volume of liquid provides a practical way to determine the object’s volume, and hence its density

Liquids at Rest.text: Which of the following correctly summarizes the overall importance of understanding density, upthrust, and Archimedes’ principle in both natural phenomena and engineering applications?
options: These concepts explain natural buoyancy phenomena (such as floating icebergs and swimming fish) and underpin engineering applications ranging from ship design to submarine operation and hydrometry
Density and Archimedes’ principle have no relevance to either natural phenomena or engineering applications
These concepts apply exclusively to theoretical physics problems with no real-world relevance
Ship and submarine design require no consideration of density or buoyancy principles
Liquids at Rest.correct_answer: These concepts explain natural buoyancy phenomena (such as floating icebergs and swimming fish) and underpin engineering applications ranging from ship design to submarine operation and hydrometry

Temperature and Its Measurement.text: Temperature is best described as a measure of
options: the total heat energy contained in a body
the degree of hotness or coldness of a body, related to the average kinetic energy of its particles
the mass of a body
the volume of a body
Temperature and Its Measurement.correct_answer: the degree of hotness or coldness of a body, related to the average kinetic energy of its particles

Temperature and Its Measurement.text: A thermometric property is a physical property that
options: remains completely constant regardless of temperature
changes measurably and predictably with temperature, allowing it to be used for temperature measurement
has no relationship to temperature whatsoever
can only be observed at absolute zero
Temperature and Its Measurement.correct_answer: changes measurably and predictably with temperature, allowing it to be used for temperature measurement

Temperature and Its Measurement.text: Which of the following is a commonly used thermometric property in a mercury-in-glass thermometer?
options: Electrical resistance
Volume expansion (or the corresponding change in length of the mercury column)
Colour change
Magnetic field strength
Temperature and Its Measurement.correct_answer: Volume expansion (or the corresponding change in length of the mercury column)

Temperature and Its Measurement.text: Calibrating a thermometer typically involves
options: marking arbitrary points with no reference to fixed physical conditions
establishing fixed reference points, such as the ice point and steam point, and dividing the scale between them
ignoring any fixed reference points entirely
using only a single reference temperature
Temperature and Its Measurement.correct_answer: establishing fixed reference points, such as the ice point and steam point, and dividing the scale between them

Temperature and Its Measurement.text: The ice point (lower fixed point) on the Celsius scale is defined as
options: 0°C, the temperature at which pure ice melts under standard atmospheric pressure
Temperature and Its Measurement.correct_answer: 0°C, the temperature at which pure ice melts under standard atmospheric pressure

Temperature and Its Measurement.text: The steam point (upper fixed point) on the Celsius scale is defined as
options: 100°C, the temperature at which pure water boils under standard atmospheric pressure
Temperature and Its Measurement.correct_answer: 100°C, the temperature at which pure water boils under standard atmospheric pressure

Temperature and Its Measurement.text: The Kelvin (absolute) temperature scale sets its zero point at
options: the ice point (0°C)
absolute zero, approximately -273°C, the theoretical point of minimum possible thermal energy
the steam point (100°C)
an arbitrary point unrelated to physical conditions
Temperature and Its Measurement.correct_answer: absolute zero, approximately -273°C, the theoretical point of minimum possible thermal energy

Temperature and Its Measurement.text: To convert a temperature from Celsius to Kelvin, one should
options: subtract 273 from the Celsius value
add 273 to the Celsius value
multiply the Celsius value by 273
divide the Celsius value by 273
Temperature and Its Measurement.correct_answer: add 273 to the Celsius value

Temperature and Its Measurement.text: A clinical (medical) thermometer is specifically designed to measure
options: extremely high industrial temperatures
human body temperature, over a relatively narrow, specific range
extremely low cryogenic temperatures
atmospheric pressure
Temperature and Its Measurement.correct_answer: human body temperature, over a relatively narrow, specific range

Temperature and Its Measurement.text: A thermocouple thermometer works based on the principle that
options: a small voltage (electromotive force) is generated at the junction of two dissimilar metals, varying predictably with temperature
mercury expands and contracts with temperature
it uses colour changes to indicate temperature
it measures atmospheric pressure rather than temperature
Temperature and Its Measurement.correct_answer: a small voltage (electromotive force) is generated at the junction of two dissimilar metals, varying predictably with temperature

Temperature and Its Measurement.text: A resistance thermometer measures temperature based on
options: changes in the electrical resistance of a conductor (typically a metal) with temperature
changes in colour with temperature
changes in volume of a liquid with temperature
changes in magnetic field strength
Temperature and Its Measurement.correct_answer: changes in the electrical resistance of a conductor (typically a metal) with temperature

Temperature and Its Measurement.text: Which of the following correctly explains why mercury, rather than water, is commonly used in liquid-in-glass thermometers?
options: Mercury remains liquid over a wide, practically useful temperature range, expands fairly uniformly with temperature, and does not wet the glass
Water has a wider useful liquid temperature range than mercury
Mercury freezes at a higher temperature than water, making it impractical for most uses
There is no meaningful advantage of mercury over water for thermometric use
Temperature and Its Measurement.correct_answer: Mercury remains liquid over a wide, practically useful temperature range, expands fairly uniformly with temperature, and does not wet the glass

Temperature and Its Measurement.text: Which of the following correctly explains why a thermocouple thermometer is often preferred for measuring very high or rapidly changing temperatures, compared to a liquid-in-glass thermometer?
options: Thermocouples can respond quickly and can be constructed to withstand and measure much higher temperatures than typical liquid-in-glass designs allow
Thermocouples are always slower to respond than liquid-in-glass thermometers
Thermocouples cannot measure high temperatures at all
There is no practical advantage of thermocouples over liquid-in-glass thermometers for high-temperature measurement
Temperature and Its Measurement.correct_answer: Thermocouples can respond quickly and can be constructed to withstand and measure much higher temperatures than typical liquid-in-glass designs allow

Temperature and Its Measurement.text: Converting 25°C to Kelvin gives approximately
Converting 373 K to Celsius gives
Which of the following correctly explains why establishing fixed reference points (such as the ice point and steam point) is essential for constructing a reliable temperature scale?
options: Fixed reference points provide known, reproducible temperature values against which the thermometric property’s scale can be accurately and consistently calibrated
Fixed reference points have no practical role in thermometer calibration
Temperature scales can be constructed reliably without any fixed reference points
Any arbitrary, non-reproducible points work equally well as fixed reference points
Temperature and Its Measurement.correct_answer: Fixed reference points provide known, reproducible temperature values against which the thermometric property’s scale can be accurately and consistently calibrated

Temperature and Its Measurement.text: Which of the following correctly explains why the Kelvin scale is generally preferred over the Celsius scale in scientific calculations involving gas laws and thermodynamics?
options: The Kelvin scale begins at absolute zero, giving a direct proportional relationship with quantities such as gas volume and pressure that would not hold using the Celsius scale, which has an arbitrary zero point
The Celsius scale is always preferred for scientific gas law calculations
There is no practical difference between using the Kelvin and Celsius scales in scientific calculations
The Kelvin scale has an arbitrary, non- physical zero point, similar to the Celsius scale
Temperature and Its Measurement.correct_answer: The Kelvin scale begins at absolute zero, giving a direct proportional relationship with quantities such as gas volume and pressure that would not hold using the Celsius scale, which has an arbitrary zero point

Temperature and Its Measurement.text: Which of the following correctly explains why a resistance thermometer, despite being more complex than a simple liquid-in-glass thermometer, is often used in industrial temperature monitoring systems?
options: Resistance thermometers can provide precise, easily digitized readings and are well-suited to continuous, automated temperature monitoring and control
Resistance thermometers are always less accurate than liquid-in-glass thermometers
Industrial systems have no need for precise or automated temperature monitoring
There is no practical advantage of resistance thermometers over liquid-in-glass designs
Temperature and Its Measurement.correct_answer: Resistance thermometers can provide precise, easily digitized readings and are well-suited to continuous, automated temperature monitoring and control

Temperature and Its Measurement.text: Which of the following correctly explains why body temperature (approximately 37°C) is measured using a clinical thermometer with a narrow temperature range, rather than a thermometer designed for a very wide range?
options: A narrow-range thermometer can provide much finer precision and readability within the specific range relevant to human body temperature
Narrow-range thermometers are always less accurate than wide-range thermometers
Body temperature measurement requires no particular precision
There is no advantage to using a narrow-range thermometer for clinical purposes
Temperature and Its Measurement.correct_answer: A narrow-range thermometer can provide much finer precision and readability within the specific range relevant to human body temperature

Temperature and Its Measurement.text: Which of the following correctly explains the general relationship between temperature and the average kinetic energy of particles in a substance, according to the kinetic theory of matter?
options: Higher temperature generally corresponds to greater average kinetic energy of the particles making up the substance
Temperature has no relationship to the kinetic energy of particles
Higher temperature always corresponds to lower average particle kinetic energy
Kinetic energy of particles is completely independent of temperature
Temperature and Its Measurement.correct_answer: Higher temperature generally corresponds to greater average kinetic energy of the particles making up the substance

Temperature and Its Measurement.text: Which of the following correctly explains why different thermometric properties (such as mercury expansion versus electrical resistance) might give slightly different readings for the same actual temperature, particularly away from the fixed calibration points?
options: Different thermometric properties do not necessarily vary in an exactly identical, linear way with true temperature, so calibration and measurement can differ slightly between different types of thermometers, especially between fixed points
All thermometric properties vary identically with temperature under all conditions
Different thermometers always give identical readings at every temperature
Thermometric property differences have no practical relevance to temperature measurement accuracy
Temperature and Its Measurement.correct_answer: Different thermometric properties do not necessarily vary in an exactly identical, linear way with true temperature, so calibration and measurement can differ slightly between different types of thermometers, especially between fixed points

Temperature and Its Measurement.text: Which of the following correctly explains why infrared (non-contact) thermometers are increasingly used in situations such as rapid temperature screening?
options: They can measure temperature quickly, without physical contact, by detecting infrared radiation emitted by the object or body being measured
Infrared thermometers require direct physical contact, similar to traditional thermometers
Infrared thermometers cannot measure temperature at all
There is no practical advantage of non- contact temperature measurement in any situation
Temperature and Its Measurement.correct_answer: They can measure temperature quickly, without physical contact, by detecting infrared radiation emitted by the object or body being measured

Temperature and Its Measurement.text: Which of the following correctly explains why temperature scales, though based on different reference points and units (such as Celsius and Fahrenheit), can be reliably converted between one another using a simple linear formula?
options: Since both scales are based on a fixed, linear relationship to the same physical phenomenon (temperature), a consistent proportional/linear conversion formula can relate readings on one scale to the other
Temperature scales cannot be reliably converted between one another
Only the Kelvin scale can be converted to other scales
Conversion between temperature scales requires no consistent mathematical relationship
Temperature and Its Measurement.correct_answer: Since both scales are based on a fixed, linear relationship to the same physical phenomenon (temperature), a consistent proportional/linear conversion formula can relate readings on one scale to the other

Temperature and Its Measurement.text: Which of the following correctly summarizes the overall importance of accurate temperature measurement and thermometry in science, industry, and everyday life?
options: Reliable temperature measurement underpins fields ranging from medicine and industrial process control to meteorology and scientific research
Temperature measurement has minimal practical importance outside of basic classroom demonstrations
Accurate thermometry is relevant only to advanced physics research, with no everyday application
Industrial and medical applications require no particular precision in temperature measurement
Temperature and Its Measurement.correct_answer: Reliable temperature measurement underpins fields ranging from medicine and industrial process control to meteorology and scientific research

Thermal Expansion.text: Linear expansivity of a solid is defined as the
options: increase in volume per unit original volume per degree rise in temperature
increase in length per unit original length per degree rise in temperature
increase in area per unit original area per degree rise in temperature
total increase in length, regardless of original length or temperature change
Thermal Expansion.correct_answer: increase in length per unit original length per degree rise in temperature

Thermal Expansion.text: Area (superficial) expansivity of a solid is defined as the
options: increase in length per unit original length per degree rise in temperature
increase in area per unit original area per degree rise in temperature
increase in volume per unit original volume per degree rise in temperature
total increase in area, regardless of original area or temperature change
Thermal Expansion.correct_answer: increase in area per unit original area per degree rise in temperature

Thermal Expansion.text: Volume (cubic) expansivity of a solid is defined as the
options: increase in length per unit original length per degree rise in temperature
increase in area per unit original area per degree rise in temperature
increase in volume per unit original volume per degree rise in temperature
unrelated to any change in temperature
Thermal Expansion.correct_answer: increase in volume per unit original volume per degree rise in temperature

Thermal Expansion.text: For most solids, the relationship between linear expansivity (α), area expansivity (β), and volume expansivity (γ) is approximately
options: β = 2α and γ = 3α
β = α and γ = α
β = 3α and γ = 2α
β and γ are unrelated to α
Thermal Expansion.correct_answer: β = 2α and γ = 3α

Thermal Expansion.text: Expansion gaps in railway lines are provided mainly to
options: increase the friction between rail sections
accommodate thermal expansion of the rails, preventing buckling in hot weather
reduce the strength of the rail track
serve no functional purpose
Thermal Expansion.correct_answer: accommodate thermal expansion of the rails, preventing buckling in hot weather

Thermal Expansion.text: Expansion joints in bridges and buildings serve mainly to
options: allow for thermal expansion and contraction of structural materials without causing damage
increase the overall rigidity of the structure with no allowance for movement
decorate the structure
reduce the structure’s overall strength
Thermal Expansion.correct_answer: allow for thermal expansion and contraction of structural materials without causing damage

Thermal Expansion.text: A bimetallic strip, used in thermostats, works based on the principle that
options: two different metals bonded together expand at identical rates, showing no bending with temperature change
two different metals bonded together have different expansivities, causing the strip to bend as temperature changes
metals do not expand with temperature at all
only one of the two metals in the strip is affected by temperature
Thermal Expansion.correct_answer: two different metals bonded together have different expansivities, causing the strip to bend as temperature changes

Thermal Expansion.text: The real expansivity of a liquid refers to the
options: apparent expansion of the liquid as observed in a container, ignoring the container’s own expansion
true expansion of the liquid itself, accounting for the expansion of the container that holds it
expansion of the container alone
expansion that occurs only in gases, not liquids
Thermal Expansion.correct_answer: true expansion of the liquid itself, accounting for the expansion of the container that holds it

Thermal Expansion.text: The apparent expansivity of a liquid refers to the
options: true, total expansion of the liquid, accounting for container expansion
expansion of the liquid as directly observed in a container, without correcting for the container’s own expansion
expansion of the solid container material alone
an expansivity value that is always identical to the real expansivity
Thermal Expansion.correct_answer: expansion of the liquid as directly observed in a container, without correcting for the container’s own expansion

Thermal Expansion.text: The relationship between real and apparent expansivity of a liquid in a container is generally
options: real expansivity = apparent expansivity − expansivity of the container
real expansivity = apparent expansivity + expansivity of the container
real expansivity = apparent expansivity, with no need to consider the container
there is no meaningful relationship between the two
Thermal Expansion.correct_answer: real expansivity = apparent expansivity + expansivity of the container

Thermal Expansion.text: The anomalous expansion of water refers to the unusual behaviour in which water
options: expands continuously and uniformly as temperature decreases from 100°C to 0°C
contracts as it is cooled from 4°C to 0°C, actually expanding rather than contracting further in this specific range
never changes volume with temperature
behaves identically to all other common liquids across all temperature ranges
Thermal Expansion.correct_answer: contracts as it is cooled from 4°C to 0°C, actually expanding rather than contracting further in this specific range

Thermal Expansion.text: Water reaches its maximum density at approximately
The anomalous expansion of water is ecologically significant mainly because it explains why
options: lakes freeze completely from the bottom up in cold weather
ice forms at the top of a body of water while liquid water (at around 4°
remains at the bottom, helping aquatic life survive freezing conditions C) water has no relevance to aquatic ecosystems
ice is always denser than liquid water
Thermal Expansion.correct_answer: ice forms at the top of a body of water while liquid water (at around 4°

Thermal Expansion.text: Which of the following correctly explains why a metal lid on a glass jar can often be loosened by running hot water over it?
options: The metal lid, generally having a higher expansivity than the glass jar, expands more than the glass upon heating, loosening its grip
Metal and glass always expand by exactly the same amount when heated
Heating a metal lid has no effect on how tightly it fits onto a glass jar
The glass jar always expands more than the metal lid when heated
Thermal Expansion.correct_answer: The metal lid, generally having a higher expansivity than the glass jar, expands more than the glass upon heating, loosening its grip

Thermal Expansion.text: Which of the following correctly explains why overhead power lines are deliberately installed with some sag, rather than being pulled perfectly taut?
options: The sag allows for thermal contraction in cold weather without the cables becoming dangerously over-tensioned or snapping
Power lines are never affected by thermal expansion or contraction
A perfectly taut installation is always preferred, with no consideration of temperature effects
Sag in power lines serves no functional purpose related to temperature changes
Thermal Expansion.correct_answer: The sag allows for thermal contraction in cold weather without the cables becoming dangerously over-tensioned or snapping

Thermal Expansion.text: Which of the following correctly explains why a bimetallic strip thermostat can be used to automatically control heating or cooling systems?
options: As temperature changes, the strip bends due to differential expansion, and this bending can be used to make or break an electrical contact, switching a heating or cooling system on or off
Bimetallic strips have no practical application in temperature control systems
Bimetallic strips remain perfectly straight regardless of temperature changes
Thermostats function without any relationship to differential thermal expansion
Thermal Expansion.correct_answer: As temperature changes, the strip bends due to differential expansion, and this bending can be used to make or break an electrical contact, switching a heating or cooling system on or off

Thermal Expansion.text: Which of the following correctly explains why measuring the true (real) expansivity of a liquid requires accounting for the expansion of its container?
options: As the liquid expands with rising temperature, the container itself also generally expands, so the directly observed (apparent) volume change underestimates the liquid’s true expansion
Containers never expand with temperature, so container expansion can always be ignored
Apparent expansivity is always identical to real expansivity, with no need for correction
Only the container’s expansion matters, with the liquid’s own real expansion being irrelevant
Thermal Expansion.correct_answer: As the liquid expands with rising temperature, the container itself also generally expands, so the directly observed (apparent) volume change underestimates the liquid’s true expansion

Thermal Expansion.text: Which of the following correctly explains why concrete and steel are often used together in reinforced concrete construction, despite being very different materials?
options: Concrete and steel have relatively similar thermal expansivities, meaning temperature changes cause the two materials to expand and contract compatibly, reducing internal stress and structural damage
Concrete and steel have vastly different expansivities, causing significant structural problems whenever used together
Thermal expansivity compatibility has no relevance to material selection in reinforced concrete construction
Steel does not expand or contract with temperature changes, unlike concrete
Thermal Expansion.correct_answer: Concrete and steel have relatively similar thermal expansivities, meaning temperature changes cause the two materials to expand and contract compatibly, reducing internal stress and structural damage

Thermal Expansion.text: Which of the following correctly explains why fitting a metal rim tightly onto a wooden cart wheel traditionally involved heating the metal rim before fitting it?
options: Heating expands the metal rim, allowing it to be more easily fitted around the wheel; as it subsequently cools and contracts, it shrinks tightly onto the wheel, creating a secure, snug fit
Heating the metal rim has no relevance to how tightly it eventually fits the wheel
The metal rim contracts, rather than expands, upon heating, making a tight fit impossible using this method
Cooling, rather than heating, would be the traditional method used to achieve a tight fit
Thermal Expansion.correct_answer: Heating expands the metal rim, allowing it to be more easily fitted around the wheel; as it subsequently cools and contracts, it shrinks tightly onto the wheel, creating a secure, snug fit

Thermal Expansion.text: Which of the following correctly explains the ecological importance of water’s anomalous expansion for aquatic organisms living in temperate or cold climates?
options: Since ice floats and forms an insulating layer at the surface, the deeper water beneath (remaining around 4°C, its densest point) stays liquid, allowing aquatic organisms to survive even when the surface freezes
Without anomalous expansion, aquatic ecosystems would be entirely unaffected by cold weather
Anomalous expansion of water has no ecological significance whatsoever
Ice always sinks to the bottom of bodies of water, according to the anomalous expansion property
Thermal Expansion.correct_answer: Since ice floats and forms an insulating layer at the surface, the deeper water beneath (remaining around 4°C, its densest point) stays liquid, allowing aquatic organisms to survive even when the surface freezes

Thermal Expansion.text: Which of the following correctly explains why railway engineers historically used to leave small gaps between sections of rail track, producing the characteristic “clickety-clack” sound of older railways?
options: These gaps accommodated thermal expansion of the rails in hot weather, preventing the rails from buckling under compressive stress
The gaps were purely decorative, with no functional relationship to thermal expansion
Rails do not expand or contract significantly with temperature changes
The gaps were designed to reduce the strength of the rail joints deliberately
Thermal Expansion.correct_answer: These gaps accommodated thermal expansion of the rails in hot weather, preventing the rails from buckling under compressive stress

Thermal Expansion.text: Which of the following correctly explains why liquid thermometers must account for the expansion of both the liquid and the glass container in their calibration?
options: Since the observed expansion in a liquid-in-glass thermometer is the apparent expansion (liquid expansion minus container expansion), accurate calibration requires accounting for both effects
Only the liquid’s expansion matters, with the glass container’s expansion having no bearing on thermometer accuracy
Only the container’s expansion matters, with the liquid’s own expansion being irrelevant
Liquid-in-glass thermometers require no consideration of either the liquid’s or the container’s expansion
Thermal Expansion.correct_answer: Since the observed expansion in a liquid-in-glass thermometer is the apparent expansion (liquid expansion minus container expansion), accurate calibration requires accounting for both effects

Thermal Expansion.text: Which of the following correctly explains why aircraft designers must carefully consider thermal expansion when designing components that experience large temperature variations during flight (from ground temperature to very cold high-altitude conditions)?
options: Differential thermal expansion and contraction of different materials and components could otherwise lead to structural stress, misalignment, or failure if not properly accounted for in the design
Thermal expansion has no relevance to aircraft design, since materials do not expand or contract significantly during flight
Temperature variations during flight are negligible and require no design consideration
All aircraft materials expand and contract identically, requiring no special design consideration
Thermal Expansion.correct_answer: Differential thermal expansion and contraction of different materials and components could otherwise lead to structural stress, misalignment, or failure if not properly accounted for in the design

Thermal Expansion.text: Which of the following correctly summarizes the overall importance of understanding thermal expansion (in solids and liquids) for engineering design and everyday technology?
options: Accounting for thermal expansion is essential in designing structures, instruments, and devices that remain safe, functional, and accurately calibrated across a range of operating temperatures
Thermal expansion has no practical relevance to engineering design or technology
Structures and devices function identically regardless of temperature-related expansion or contraction effects
Only theoretical physics benefits from understanding thermal expansion, with no real-world engineering application
Thermal Expansion.correct_answer: Accounting for thermal expansion is essential in designing structures, instruments, and devices that remain safe, functional, and accurately calibrated across a range of operating temperatures

Gas Laws.text: Boyle’s law, describing an isothermal process, states that at constant temperature, the pressure of a fixed mass of gas is
options: directly proportional to its volume
inversely proportional to its volume
independent of its volume
directly proportional to the square of its volume
Gas Laws.correct_answer: inversely proportional to its volume

Gas Laws.text: Boyle’s law is mathematically expressed as
options: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂
V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂
P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂
PV = nRT only
Gas Laws.correct_answer: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂

Gas Laws.text: Charles’ law, describing an isobaric process, states that at constant pressure, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is
options: inversely proportional to its absolute temperature
directly proportional to its absolute temperature
independent of temperature
directly proportional to pressure
Gas Laws.correct_answer: directly proportional to its absolute temperature

Gas Laws.text: Charles’ law is mathematically expressed as
options: V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂
P₁V₁ = P₂V₂
P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂
V₁P₁ = V₂P₂
Gas Laws.correct_answer: V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂

Gas Laws.text: The pressure law, describing an isochoric (constant volume) process, states that at constant volume, the pressure of a fixed mass of gas is
options: inversely proportional to its absolute temperature
directly proportional to its absolute temperature
independent of temperature
directly proportional to volume
Gas Laws.correct_answer: directly proportional to its absolute temperature

Gas Laws.text: The pressure law is mathematically expressed as
options: P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂
P₁V₁ = P₂V₂
V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂
PV = constant, independent of temperature
Gas Laws.correct_answer: P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂

Gas Laws.text: Absolute zero is the theoretical temperature at which
options: gas particles would have maximum kinetic energy
an ideal gas’s volume and pressure would theoretically become zero, and particle motion would be minimized
water boils
water freezes
Gas Laws.correct_answer: an ideal gas’s volume and pressure would theoretically become zero, and particle motion would be minimized

Gas Laws.text: Absolute zero corresponds to approximately
The general gas equation, combining Boyle’s, Charles’, and the pressure law, is expressed as
options: PV/T = constant, for a fixed mass of gas
P + V + T = constant
P − V − T = constant
PVT = constant
Gas Laws.correct_answer: PV/T = constant, for a fixed mass of gas

Gas Laws.text: The ideal gas equation is expressed as
options: PV = nRT
PT = nRV
PV = RT/n
nT = PVR
Gas Laws.correct_answer: PV = nRT

Gas Laws.text: In the ideal gas equation PV = nRT, n represents the
options: pressure of the gas
number of moles of gas
absolute temperature
universal gas constant
Gas Laws.correct_answer: number of moles of gas

Gas Laws.text: In the ideal gas equation PV = nRT, R represents the
options: number of moles
universal (molar) gas constant
absolute temperature
volume of the gas
Gas Laws.correct_answer: universal (molar) gas constant

Gas Laws.text: A gas that behaves according to the ideal gas equation under all conditions is called
options: a real gas
an ideal gas, which is a useful theoretical approximation
a liquid
a solid
Gas Laws.correct_answer: an ideal gas, which is a useful theoretical approximation
